source.title: Modular Pretraining Enables Access Control
source.authors: Ethan Roland; Murat Cubuktepe; Eric L Martinez; Stijn Servaes; Keenan Pepper; Michael Vaiana; D. D. de Lucena; Judd Rosenblatt; Addie Foote; Cem Anil; Alex Cloud

page_placements.theme: Robustness defenses and alternatives, and the limits of their robustness

record.tranche_reason: The study directly tests post-hoc unlearning under fine-tuning elicitation. Its results say MaxEnt's forgetting is mostly reversed, while modular pretraining methods resist the tested elicitation better; it therefore refines the claim by distinguishing methods.
record.gate_note: Rows record the study's own compute-ratio results and fine-tuning elicitation results. Mentions of vulnerabilities and results from cited work are not recorded as findings from this study. The study does not test quantization or prompt-only recovery.
record.test_reason: The study runs post-hoc unlearning (MaxEnt) at 26M and 800M parameters, then fine-tunes on forget-category samples. Its own numbers show the removal is almost fully reversed, which bears on A and B. It also proposes GRAM, a pretraining modular method, and reports that GRAM resists the same elicitation about as well as data filtering, which bears on F. It measures cross-entropy compute ratios, not accuracy against chance. It does not test internal edits, quantization or prompting.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but the final clause about quantization and prompting is the reader's comment, not the authors'. The authors conclude: GRAM approximates many data-filtered models in one run. GRAM resists fine-tuning recovery about as well as filtering and far better than post-hoc unlearning, whose forgetting is mostly reversed. Data filtering scales favorably, and GRAM and FT-LoRA track it up to 5B. GRAM also composes capabilities better and handles partial labeling better.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes GRAM, a pretraining method that localizes capabilities in auxiliary modules and removes them by inference-time ablation. It compares this with post-hoc MaxEnt unlearning and tests fine-tuning elicitation; it does not reproduce the original unlearning recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Fine-tuning elicitation results depend on method. In the Simple Stories sweep, GRAM's elicited-forget performance rises modestly with more auxiliary categories. The scaling analysis reports increasing robustness to elicitation with model scale.

fits_no_version.finding: Data-filtered models learn the excluded domain less and resist fine-tuning elicitation more as scale grows from 50M to 5B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretraining data filtering yields removal whose robustness to fine-tuning elicitation improves with model scale.

fits_no_version.finding: With 50% of data labeled, GRAM's forget CR (0.60) is far below filtering's and FT-LoRA's (0.85).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient-routed modular pretraining removes capabilities better than filtering under partial labels.

record.problems: The study measures cross-entropy-derived compute ratios rather than accuracy relative to chance. The Simple Stories experiment is synthetic and small (26M parameters); the realistic dual-use experiment is 800M parameters, and the scaling experiment reaches 5B. For the scaling sweep, only one run was done at 2B and 5B. The authors also note that cross-entropy may not fully represent downstream performance.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 7 presents individual per-size values for the scaling sweep, but the accompanying text reports the trend rather than clearly attributable exact values; the aggregate text-described result is recorded in G1–G3 instead of transcribing separate figure-only points.

untested.parts: Accuracy against chance is not measured (cross-entropy compute ratios only); prompt-based and other simple attacks are not tested; only one unlearning method (MaxEnt) is tested.
Relearning on unrelated or loosely related data is not tested; only samples from the forget categories are used.
Entirely untested: no activation-direction ablation and no analysis showing MaxEnt blocks access rather than deleting.
Rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages and in-context recovery are not tested.
GRAM's robustness to quantization, prompting and larger elicitation budgets is not tested; the authors model a limited adversary.

missing.what: Per-method 800M compute ratios, especially MaxEnt forget versus elicited forget. The extracted bar labels cannot be attributed reliably; MaxEnt forget may be about 0.46 and elicit about 0.9.
GRAM auxiliary-spread sweep: forget/elicit rise from 0.69/0.78 at pas=0 to 0.89/0.97 at pas=1. Core-robustness sweep: elicit 0.90→0.83.
Elicited forget under partial labeling and in the 100M architecture ablation (GRAM MLP vs LoRA).

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The C link on S4 was removed: the 'remains encoded' remark is inferred from fine-tuning recovery. Filtering, FT-LoRA and FT-Full rows were relinked to none; they are not unlearning methods. The filtering rise serves as the control for B and F. Elicitation uses a limited budget (75 steps / 512 sequences), and the authors expect partial recovery even from filtered models with more data. Measures are cross-entropy compute ratios, not benchmark accuracy. Only one run was done at 2B and 5B.

versions.untested_parts: It evaluates capability loss and retention with compute ratios, not accuracy against chance; the tested elicitation is fine-tuning, not every simple attack.
Fine-tuning uses samples from the forgotten categories; unrelated or loosely related examples and rephrasing are not tested.
No activation-direction ablation is tested. The relevant evidence is the authors' interpretation that post-hoc-unlearned capabilities remain encoded after recovery by fine-tuning.
Low-bit quantization recovery is not tested.
Prompt rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, and in-context recovery are not tested.
Robustness is tested against fine-tuning elicitation, not quantization or prompt-only attacks.
